# §M — Deployment, project-memory federation, and Crier directors
**CHD-3.5 revision notice (readiness/fencing):** This chapter supersedes any CHD-3.3 claim that scheduler registration is a universal startup or dispatch prerequisite. Read-only, immediate, and scheduled readiness are separate capabilities. Immediate admission still requires the authoritative attempt/run reservation and storage-boundary fence/snapshot; federation and local project memory cannot provide a second ledger.

## M.0 Deployment readiness contract
A deployment publishes `read_only_ready`, `immediate_ready`, and `scheduled_ready` separately. Read-only requires authenticated authoritative reads and durable control readback. Immediate additionally requires the configured admission owner, correlated attempt/run reservation, storage-boundary fencing and authoritative snapshot support, profile/credential/runtime checks, and gateway capability readback. Scheduled additionally requires scheduler registration/readback for every lane. A scheduler outage therefore sets scheduled readiness false and leaves triggers unarmed, but does not globally block read-only or an otherwise-ready controller-local immediate request. Scheduler-owner admission mode remains blocked until scheduler approval is healthy.
The reservation owner is the controller's authoritative attempt/run ledger. Manifest, report, board, role, local project-memory, and scheduler counters are projections or trigger state and cannot release capacity. A report, waiting state, timeout, cancellation intent, process absence, or network response is not stop proof. Release requires a correlated authoritative attempt/run terminal status or trusted runtime stop attestation, then a durable release readback. If the fencing/snapshot adapter is unavailable or unresolved, immediate and scheduled readiness remain false; the controller does not invent native DuckBrain transaction or CAS semantics.

## M.0.1 Native and storage release gates
The required native `hermes.session.export` export/import adapter, supported API/version, request/response/error contract, response-loss reconciliation and export → import → first-turn trace remain OPEN-ARCHIVE-1 until probed and verified. The storage LeaseAuthority/FencedStore/SnapshotToken binding likewise remains open until atomic reservation/fence binding, stale-writer rejection at the write boundary, durable high-water reads and multi-page snapshot consistency are evidenced. These unresolved release gates are visible in readiness readback; no fallback raw SQLite ledger, guessed payload format, or guessed native API is permitted.
**Status:** deployment and federation contract for CHD-3.5.
**Authority.** This chapter maps VOL-D §§1.10 and 5.1–5.6 (`VOLD-037..042`, `VOLD-056..059`, `VOLD-085..089`), VOL-B §§1 and 6.6, VOL-C §8, R31-028 and R31-029. It defines deployment routing, not a new ticket or permission state machine. `schemas/federation-map.schema.json` governs peer mapping and `schemas/bridge-envelope.schema.json` governs bridge delivery.

## M.1 Four data classes and one default route
The controller DuckBrain route is the default for tool calls. Data classes are separate even when they use the same controller service:
TABLE 13.1-1 — M.1 Four data classes and one default route
| Class | Default backend | Consistency | Can acknowledge completion? | |---|---|---|---| | `coordination_report` | controller `/chd` | immediate, `fsync` | yes, after controller readback | | `control_key` | controller `/chd` | immediate, `fsync` | yes, after controller readback | | `session_archive` | controller `/chd-archive` ingestor | checkpointed | only after archive commit/readback | | `project_code_memory` | disabled by default; controller, local, or federated | eventual/background | **never** by itself |
A completion report and control transition always use the controller path. A local observation may be queued or stale while sync runs; it cannot be used as the acknowledgement of a report, grant, ticket, lease, or verdict. If the controller is unavailable, the operation returns `503 control_store_unavailable` and remains queued/blocked; no completion is manufactured.

## M.2 Two supported storage topologies
**T-A central-only (default).** Agents proxy all control, report, archive, and project-memory reads/writes to the controller. This gives one immediate readback authority and no project-memory replication lag.
**T-B central control plus local/federated project memory.** Agents still proxy coordination/report and control-key tools to the controller. A configured project namespace may be local or federated. In the local topology, the controller accepts the observation request, but the named **local project-memory writer** is the component that writes the local project-memory store under its local-store credential; the controller does not write that store directly. The named single **project-memory sync owner** owns checkpointing, conflict policy, and retry, and reports the sync checkpoint/result back through the controller. The same writer/sync-owner separation applies at a configured federated project backend. Conflicts use `controller_wins` for central keys and `local_wins_on_project_keys` for project-only keys; every conflict is durable and retried from `last_synced_rev/ts`, never silently discarded.
The two drawings are deliberately separate: `fig-storage-topology.svg` and its Mermaid source show the immediate controller path, checkpointed archive path, and optional eventual project-memory path. Their arrows label backend, proxy, acknowledgement, and lag. A deployment cannot silently change T-A into T-B. `GET /v1/effective-routing` reads back, per class, backend, namespace, sync, proxy, credential reference name, digest, sync owner, and project lag.

## M.3 Route configuration and failure behavior Configuration names classes explicitly: ```json { "storage": { "classes": { "coordination_report": {"namespace":"chd","backend":"controller","sync":"immediate","proxy":"controller"}, "control_key": {"namespace":"chd","backend":"controller","sync":"immediate","proxy":"controller"}, "session_archive": {"namespace":"chd-archive","backend":"controller","sync":"checkpointed","proxy":"archive-ingestor"}, "project_code_memory": {"namespace":"project-alpha","backend":"local","sync":"background","proxy":"controller"} }, "controller": {"backend_url":"https://controller.example/v1","credential_ref_name":"ctrl-api"}, "sync": {"owner":"controller-sync-1","conflict":"controller_wins"} } } ``` Unknown classes, credentials embedded in configuration, or a control class pointing at a delayed backend fail validation. Startup checks config, controller reachability, achieved durability, registry/bond mirrors, and zero traffic before arming triggers. Each write confirms `X-Durability` is the configured `fsync` mode; a degraded barrier is a loud failure, not an acknowledgement. TABLE 13.1-2 — M.3 Route configuration and failure behavior | Failure | Immediate effect | Recovery/evidence | |---|---|---| | controller unavailable | no control/report dispatch; `503 control_store_unavailable` | retry same request id after health/readback; report remains blocked | | local project store unavailable | observation read/write is stale or queued | show lag; do not affect controller completion | | sync conflict | conflict record, no silent winner | apply configured class rule, retry from checkpoint, read back digest | | archive ingestor unavailable | live control continues; checkpoint/gap remains visible | resume capture; do not claim coverage beyond last commit | | peer bridge unavailable | federation traffic isolated | local objectives, tickets, reports and workers continue | FIGURE 13.3-1 — ROUTE FAILURE / RECOVERY — PRODUCER TO CONSUMER. The route keeps the producer obligation visible until the controller consumer reads back a correlated durable result. Branch A holds the same request when the queue or controller is unavailable; branch B sends a rejected report to rework rather than manufacturing completion; branch C permits advancement only after verified recovery and acknowledgement.

## M.4 Crier: independent directors, not a hierarchy shortcut Crier connects independent director systems under different owners. Each system retains its own VP, director, managers, supervisors, foremen, workers, local policy, control store, and acceptance. A peer is an authenticated external principal such as `crier:client-alpha`, mapped to a local actor `peer:client-alpha` by a durable `FederationMap`. Connectivity never confers VP status. A message claiming `as: vp` is rejected with `403 peer_vp_claim` and audited. Trust is only the configured transport identity and scope. A peer request cannot create a local grant, bypass a local approval, write local DuckBrain, or alter local VP configuration. Onboarding records the peer key/token reference, owner label, expiry, allowed objective/message/room/ticket scopes, automatic-vs-proposal mode, approval route, local actor, and dedupe namespace. Local owner policy is evaluated after authentication and before any objective, ticket, dispatch, grant, or report side effect: - allowed scope may create a correlated local objective/ticket; - proposal-only or approval-gated scope becomes `202 pending_local_approval`; - untrusted, expired, malformed, or out-of-scope work is `403` with only an audit record, or `202` if local policy explicitly chooses wait; - no peer request is allowed to widen local VP bounds. FIGURE 13.5-1 — PEER SCOPE / LOCAL APPROVAL BOUNDARY. The peer producer supplies identity and requested scope; the local consumer decides allow or deny. Out-of-scope work produces an auditable denial and no dispatch, while connectivity never supplies local VP approval. The figure is read left to right by the local policy consumer. Identity is authenticated before scope is evaluated; an allow edge maps the peer to a local actor, while the deny edge produces an audit-only result and blocks dispatch. This boundary preserves local approval ownership even when the bridge transport is healthy.

## M.5 Bridge directions and durable delivery
Crier bridge traffic has distinct planes and arrows. They must not be collapsed.
**Inbound data/read/lease:** Crier inbox → bridge authentication and scope check → lease claim → inbound dedupe → controller local objective/message/report write. The lease is held until the local durable write and dedupe result are known. A malformed or unauthorized inbound payload is dead-lettered and never partially posted.
**Outbound ACK:** after the local room/objective/report write has received the configured durability acknowledgement, the bridge sends an ACK containing the same `delivery_id`, local record key, durability mode, and outcome. ACK is not an outbound topic publication and does not authorize work.
**Outbound topic/inbox delivery:** local event → bridge envelope → configured Crier topic or durable peer inbox. The destination is explicit; important work uses a durable inbox, while topic delivery is only for configured relay events. A topic publication is not evidence that the peer performed work.
The bridge consumes only authenticated, scoped input and produces a durable local record before its ACK producer acts. A lease expiry re-enters the dedupe consumer; a repeated delivery replays the prior ACK and does not create a second effect. A bounded retry exhaustion produces one dead-letter record and one outage record for the outage window; it does not manufacture completion.
Every envelope carries `delivery_id`, `peer_request_id` where applicable, `origin`, source system, target scope, schema version, and payload digest. Retries reuse the same delivery id and request id. The receiver stores a dedupe result before forwarding work; repeated delivery replays the prior ACK and creates no second objective, ticket, room message, lease, or external effect. Lease expiry causes redelivery, not duplicate work. Bounded retry exhaustion writes a dead-letter record and one outage/incident record per outage window. Origin tags prevent a bridge from re-egressing its own inbound message.
The bridge is not in the controller's transaction. A successful network response is not cross-system commit; read back local records and correlate the peer request/report. See `fig-crier-bridge.svg` and its Mermaid source for the separate inbound and outbound sequences.

## M.6 Correlation and approval example
`peer_request_id=pr-42` from `client-alpha` authenticates, maps to `peer:client-alpha`, passes local scope, and creates `obj-local-42` and `ticket-42`. Every local report carries `peer_request_id`, `ticket_id`, a report digest, and `peer_report_id=rr-42`. A retry of `pr-42` resolves the existing mapping. A request for `room:private` produces `403 peer_scope_denied` (or a policy-selected pending record) without local dispatch. If approval is required, local VP approval is recorded before work; peer connectivity does not supply it.
The internal “same owner asks its own director to re-enter a cycle” path is not peer federation and keeps local provenance. Crier moves scoped work and reports; it does not imply project-memory replication. Project-memory federation remains independently configured and independently granted.

## M.7 Required evidence and runbooks An operator must be able to read back: effective routing digest; backend and namespace per class; `fsync` durability; sync owner and lag; conflict records; peer mapping revision and scope; local approval/deny; inbound lease and dedupe; ACK durability mode; outbound destination; retry count; dead-letter key; outage window; and correlated local/peer report ids. `runbooks/peer-onboarding.md` covers trust and scope. `runbooks/bridge-deadletter.md` covers retry and dead-letter recovery. `examples/bridge/inbound-data-outbound-ack/` proves the inbound data/read/lease sequence and later outbound ACK. The `untrusted-peer/` fixture proves `peer_vp_claim`, scope denial, and approval hold. `outage-isolation/` proves repeated delivery is idempotent and local work continues while bridge delivery is down. **Full-size figure detail:** FIGURE 13.1-1, FIGURE 13.4-1 in §27; the detail sheets carry the drawing, explanation, steps and failure branches.
